grade.first_issue: In Case 3's second subcase, the claim that repeatedly cutting the largest angle must eventually make the largest angle less than 180°−θ or equal to θ is unsupported and false. For θ=90° and angles (60°,100°,20°), such cuts merely transfer 90° between angles, so one angle remains greater than 90° indefinitely.
grade.summary: The final characterization is correct, and much of the sufficiency argument is sound. The second subcase of sufficiency has a false termination claim, although it could be repaired locally: after its first cut, the angle β−θ already satisfies (β−θ)+θ=β<180°, so the preceding subcase applies. More seriously, necessity rests entirely on the unproved and explicitly false assertion that every W_k is a countable union of lines for any θ. Projection after eliminating the cut parameter can impose no condition on the parent when the two child equations become dependent; the proof does not classify or exclude this degeneracy under θ≠180°/n. Thus the central necessity direction is not established as submitted.
strengths: The claimed answer θ=180°/n for integers n≥2 is correct.
Peeling an angle kθ into θ and (k−1)θ is a valid strategy.
The reduction when all angles exceed θ is essentially correct: the retained nonterminal child has a new smallest angle decreased by θ.
The first subcase for an angle γ<θ correctly constructs one terminal child and another containing (n−1)θ.
The recursive definition of bounded-depth winning sets is conceptually appropriate.

errors.description: The termination assertion in the second subcase of Case 3 is false. It can be repaired with a short different observation, but that observation is absent.

The countable-union-of-lines induction in the necessity proof does not handle dependent child constraints whose elimination becomes an identity. The statement is even claimed for every θ, contradicting the already-proved sufficiency cases; for example, when θ=90°, the conditions x=90° and 180°−x=90° coincide and yield an open set of winning parents. Merely saying the other child condition still restricts the parent does not prove the required nondegeneracy for θ≠180°/n.
